analysis.one_liner: Lets bankruptcy courts reduce mortgage balances and freeze adjustable rates for struggling homeowners.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The HOMES Act would have let homeowners in Chapter 13 bankruptcy get help with mortgages on their primary homes. If a lender agreed in writing, a judge could cut the loan balance down to the home's current value. For lower-income homeowners, the court could also waive prepayment penalties and block, delay, or cancel interest-rate increases on adjustable-rate mortgages, and could treat undisclosed interest and fees as cancelable. It would also let homeowners whose lender had started foreclosure delay the required pre-bankruptcy credit counseling, and it directed a government study of the effects on the mortgage secondary market. Changes applied only to loans made before September 26, 2007 and sunset after seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: Lower- and middle-income homeowners whose primary residence was headed into foreclosure, especially those with adjustable-rate mortgages: they could freeze or cancel rate hikes, escape prepayment penalties, and — with their lender's written agreement — reduce the loan balance to what the home was actually worth. Homeowners facing foreclosure could also file for bankruptcy without first completing credit counseling.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a Chapter 13 bankruptcy court to lower the principal on a primary-residence mortgage to the home's fair market value, but only if the debtor and the mortgage holder agree in writing [S2][S3].

Lets the court waive prepayment penalties and prohibit, delay, or cancel interest-rate adjustments on adjustable-rate mortgages for debtors below specified income limits — with no lender consent required [S2][S3].
Lets a court treat interest, late fees, or other fees tied to a substantial failure to disclose loan terms as voidable transfers, so lenders could not profit from terms they hid [S2][S3].

Lets a homeowner whose lender has started foreclosure delay the required pre-bankruptcy credit counseling until after filing, so they are not locked out of bankruptcy protection while a foreclosure proceeds [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and investors in mortgage-backed securities, who would give up prepayment penalties, some adjustable-rate increases, and fees tied to undisclosed terms on covered loans. To the extent the changes raised expected losses on mortgages, future borrowers could face somewhat higher rates or tighter lending.

drawbacks.text: The bill's biggest potential benefit — cutting the loan balance to the home's value — required the mortgage holder's written agreement, so a lender could simply refuse and the provision would do nothing for the homeowner [S2][S3].

Letting courts void adjustable-rate increases and fees could make mortgage lending riskier or less predictable, which lenders and investors in the secondary market warned would be priced into costs for future homebuyers — a concern the bill itself acknowledged by ordering a Comptroller General study of the impact on the secondary mortgage market [S2][S3].
The relief was narrow: it applied only to mortgages initiated before September 26, 2007, only to debtors below specified income thresholds, and only for seven years after enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For homeowners drowning in mortgages worth less than they owed, the bill offered real but limited help: the rate freezes, penalty waivers, and disclosure-fee provisions worked without lender consent, but the principal-reduction provision — the part that mattered most in a collapsing housing market — was toothless unless the lender agreed. The costs fell on mortgage lenders and investors, with a plausible pass-through to future borrowers that the bill's own study requirement flagged.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2007, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never moved — no hearing, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the HOMES Act on October 3, 2007, as mortgage defaults and foreclosures were climbing nationwide [S1][S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; two Republican senators signed on as cosponsors [S1][S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no committee markups, no floor action — through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors holding home loans were better off, since no court could have lowered balances, waived penalties, or frozen their adjustable rates. Homeowners facing foreclosure in 2007–2008 got no bankruptcy relief from this bill as the foreclosure wave worsened.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

against.name: Mortgage lending industry
against.role: Lenders, servicers, and mortgage-backed securities investors
against.what_they_did: Opposed bankruptcy-court restructuring of home mortgages throughout this era, arguing it would raise borrowing costs and disrupt the secondary mortgage market — a concern the bill's own study provision reflects

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with two Republican cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded; the outcome was decided by committee inaction, not by a recorded division.

industries.note: The bill would have let courts waive prepayment penalties and freeze or cancel adjustable-rate increases on covered loans, and treat undisclosed fees as voidable — money lenders would otherwise collect from distressed homeowners. Its main benefit to homeowners (principal reduction) required the lender's written consent, which sharply limited the loss.

industries.industry: Mortgage-backed securities investors and the secondary mortgage market
industries.note: Rewriting mortgage terms in bankruptcy reduces expected cash flows on loans bundled into securities. The bill directed the Comptroller General to study exactly this impact, showing lawmakers saw the secondary market as the party bearing the cost.
